Through a bedroom door: Dvij and the yogini sitting together on the bed. In the foreground Bhavi stands half behind a curtain, watching, her face empty.
A close-up of Bhavi at the curtain.
The curtain falling back as she goes.
Dvij stands with a hand out, talking; the yogini sits on the bed listening.

Dvij in profile, ribbons of his own words curling round him: your beauty bewitches me; we cannot have any of this nonsense; the other girl, I sort of like her; the way moonlight plays with your hair; good night, you'll sleep, then I will.
The yogini looks back at him, not understanding a word.
Dvij steps out into the courtyard and wipes his forehead, relieved.
Bhavi's shape in a lit doorway behind him.
Across the courtyard, Ponga sprawled asleep on the flagstones, snoring, with musical notes floating over him.
The lodge from above at night: a courtyard house round a planted square, its rooms lit one by one - Ponga asleep on the flagstones, the yogini in a doorway, a single lamp burning behind one shutter.
Dvij stands at a door in the colonnade with his hand raised to knock, the moon behind him.
Bhavi lies half-reclining on a rolling bolster staring at nothing; Dvij stands in the open doorway behind her.
Dvij crosses to a plastic chair by the door.
Dvij sits down small in the chair; Bhavi turns away from him and opens a book under the lamp.
A run of narrow panels: Bhavi lying on her side, turning over, reading, turning the page, shifting again - and a small blue frame of her curled up asleep.
Bhavi is on her feet with both hands on her hips, demanding to know what he thinks he is doing.
Dvij, in the chair, points at himself - who, me?
Bhavi shouts at him, hair flying.
Dvij spreads a hand and explains that the girl was freezing on the pavement and he merely suggested she sleep in his bed; Bhavi stands over him with her back to us.
Bhavi looks back over her shoulder at him, unreadable.
Dvij talks from the chair about what the Professor would have called her; Bhavi stands at the far wall with her back to him, beside the lamp and the bed.
Two narrow frames of Dvij shifting uncomfortably in the chair.
Two narrow frames of Bhavi facing the wall, hands moving aimlessly.
A sliver of her sleeve.
Bhavi turns on him and asks whether he is going to apologise.
Dvij, both hands out, protests that she told him not to say anything.
Bhavi raises a finger - she did not say he could not apologise.
Dvij lowers his head, a hand flat on his chest, and says he is sorry.
Bhavi, half smiling despite herself.
Bhavi at the window with her back turned; Dvij still in the chair across the room.
Dvij gets up from the chair; Bhavi comes past with a folded cloth.
Bhavi bends to pick something up; Dvij watches from the chair.
Bhavi with a hand at her chest.
A close-up of Bhavi, looking back at him, almost amused.
Dvij sits hunched in the chair, scratching at the calluses on his foot.
Bhavi and Dvij in profile facing each other across the room, a brass lamp between them.
Bhavi stands by the lamp table telling him what she has been thinking about; Dvij sits in the chair listening.
A sliver of Bhavi's hair.
Bhavi looks back at him; Dvij's face close, waiting.
The two of them close together, Bhavi saying she does not believe any of it - excepting what he has just said.
The two of them walking out into the night, the gate ahead, stars overhead.
The Milky Way spilled across the whole sky above them; Dvij and Bhavi stand small beneath it, facing each other.
The gravel path and the creaking gate behind them - and below, the town at night with a river of lamps winding up through it to a lit temple tower.
Dvij's face, watching the procession.
Dvij looks up at the sky, troubled.
Bhavi looking up beside him.
Dvij in profile.
Bhavi asks why so serious.
Dvij sits down among the great spreading roots of a banyan; Bhavi stands nearby under the stars.
Bhavi listening.
Dvij sits back against the roots, looking up; Bhavi stands over him.
Dvij talks with a hand raised, then in close-up, saying the valley pulsates with suffering and asking how he is to save people who do not wish to be saved.
Dvij and Bhavi close together in the dark.
The two of them sitting in the roots; beside them a chart of the kundalini - a seated figure with the seven chakras named up the spine from muladhara to sahasrara, a serpent coiled at the base.
The two sitting together; beside them a painting of Krishna driving Arjuna's chariot into battle.
Dvij and Bhavi close, she leaning in to tell him not to worry.
The two of them small among the banyan roots, looking out over the lit valley under the stars.
Morning chaos in the lodge: Dvij crouched over a half-packed bag, Ponga squatting among the clutter, Kurup stooping at the back, the yogini in the doorway.
Dvij and Bhavi, now in a rust-red shirt, stand before a wall of framed god-prints - Ganesha at the centre - with a lamp burning beneath them and brass vessels on the shelves.
Dvij and Bhavi talking to the cook, who looks doubtful.
The send-off breakfast: a stack of ghee-soaked parathas with butter melting on top, tumblers of milk, bowls of curd and pickle.
The Professor asleep in bed under a white sheet, still bandaged, a lamp on the table beside him.
The party walks out through the lodge gates with packs on their backs - Dvij, Bhavi, Kurup, Ponga and the yogini - looking back at the house.

A bullock cart piled with bundles jolting along a green track, the whole party hanging on: the yogini and Bhavi at the back, Ponga wedged between them, Kurup and the driver up front, two white bullocks straining ahead.
A strip of five faces in a row - Kurup, Dvij, Ponga, the yogini and Bhavi - each reacting to the ride.
Unloading in the forest: bundles handed down, the cart turning back, the party gathering under the canopy, Kurup pointing the way on and telling them the rest is on foot.
The group moves fast through the forest behind Kurup, who strides ahead; Ponga totters at the back with his staff.
Kurup turns back down the trail to wait for the stragglers.
Dvij and the yogini close together; Bhavi at the edge of the frame, watching.
Bhavi with her arms folded, looking away, unconvinced.

The trees end. Mount Dronagiri rises sheer out of a wide plain of yellow grass into a blue sky, snow on its highest ridges. The whole party stops and tilts their heads back - all except Kurup, who crouches at the grass.
Kurup pats at the grass, checking the ground. An inset shows cattle floundering in a sinkhole.
Kurup points out the hidden tribal trail; the party walks along it in single file through the grass.

The far end of the plain: a stepped tank beside a small white shrine with a vermilion Hanuman seated inside. Langurs sit in the trees, the water is muddy and covered in pink lotus. Dvij stands looking at it, Kurup crouches, Ponga lies in the grass, the yogini leans on her spear and Bhavi kneels at the water's edge.
Dvij and Bhavi sit together on the stone edge of the tank, lotus pads on the water, the mountain beyond.
The shrine with its vermilion Hanuman and a pair of boots left on the step; and Dvij in close-up, saying the Professor would like this spot.
Bhavi, looking up.
The two of them on the bank with the whole view behind - pond, lotus, plain and mountain - Dvij talking about open spaces.
Bhavi asking how he knew.
Dvij's face.
A panel headed Dvij remembers: the same pond and mountain seen again, and the two of them sitting on the bank.

The flashback proper: on the lodge lawn the Professor flings an arm up towards the orange flag on the roof, telling Dvij the lodge is Arjuna's chariot and he is Parthasarathi waiting for a deserving Arjuna. Dvij stands listening, his head still bandaged.
A painting of Krishna driving Arjuna's chariot; the Professor reaching up with an open hand; the flag snapping at the top of its pole.
Dvij, bandaged, unsure how to answer.
The Professor, delighted that he asks questions at all.
The Professor, one finger raised, talking about centuries of submissiveness; Dvij seated beside him. An inset of two open hands, and the words wofully inadequate written small.
Dvij, head bandaged, a hand at his chin, asking where this valley actually is.
The Professor raises a finger: it could be anywhere, and yet it is nowhere.
Dvij repeating the word back - nowhere?
The Professor at his desk with his hands pressed together, saying it might not even exist.
The Professor flings an arm out towards the far hills, telling Dvij about mesolithic paintings in the depths of the Bhoodara caves; Dvij turns to look.
The Professor talks with an open hand on the lodge lawn. Beside him, a painted cave interior: red-and-green figures of hunters and animals on the rock, people at a fire.
The Professor with his fingertips at his lips, Dvij beside him. Three framed insets: a wooded hillside, villagers round a large pot, and a seated assembly of elders.

Two frames of the Professor telling Dvij about the Bahlika culture found in the valley - that they ate beef with garlic and drank an intoxicant called gauda. Insets show a robed king, people at a cooking pot, and a still-life of a jar with garlic and onions.
The Professor, close to Dvij's ear, says Charvaka's texts were not destroyed and he has found some in this very valley. Beside them, framed scenes of seated gatherings by lamplight.

A large hand-drawn chart headed The Valley - A Microcosm of the Universe, Preserving Every Stage of Indian Religious Thought: the mountain at the centre with shrines and sites labelled around it, roundels of ascetics and deities linked by lines, and a row of small scenes along the bottom. The Professor spreads both hands towards it while Dvij looks on.
A strip of three reaction shots - the Professor, Dvij, the Professor with a hand raised - and then the Professor hurrying away across the lawn calling for solace, Dvij left sitting in the chair.

The vantage point: the party on the terrace by the Hanuman shrine with the pushkarini behind them, Mount Dronagiri filling the sky ahead - a jagged south-east face and a gentler green north-west slope. Kurup stands pointing out the Himapan forest that lies between; an eagle turns over the water.
Kurup, finger raised, says the forest has a beast even the Nagas fear. Below, an inset of Naga tribesmen with spears among the trees.
Dvij asks what beast. Below him, a plain view of the bamboo.
Kurup taps his own scarred cheek: the same forest where a tiger did this to him. Below, an inset of a tiger coming through the undergrowth, snarling.
At the edge of a bamboo grove, Kurup talks with Dvij and Bhavi; the yogini sits on a rock behind and Ponga squats at the right. Beyond them the forest goes dark and dense.
Kurup, Dvij and Bhavi in the bamboo: they cannot risk going into the forest.
Dvij looks up, suggesting they walk around it.
Bhavi, close, says it is too risky - the Mahant's men will spot them.
Kurup asks what to do then.
Bhavi, furious, one finger up, asks whether Dvij can get the yogini to leave the same way he got her into his bed.
Kurup's eyes go wide; Dvij looks caught out; Bhavi puts a hand to her chest, regretting it.

Dvij and Bhavi in the bamboo, Ponga tottering behind: they cannot move fast enough with him, and cannot go slowly for fear of being seen with her. Dvij points; Bhavi folds her arms; the yogini stands at the right.
Dvij and Bhavi at the forest edge with a dark dog beside them.
The yogini gathers herself up and walks off into the bamboo with her spear; Bhavi turns to watch; Ponga follows, leaning on a chewed bamboo pole, the dog trailing after.
A row of five close faces down the page: Bhavi, curious; Dvij, wondering where he is off to; Kurup, appalled; Bhavi again, seeing it; and Dvij confirming it.
The bamboo closes over a narrow path. Kurup throws out a hand, Dvij and Bhavi stand in the trail, and far ahead the two small figures walk on into the dark.
The three of them left standing at the edge, each with a thought bubble: Kurup sees the Mahant's face; Bhavi sees herself with the Professor; Dvij sees himself with Bhavi.
Bhavi recoils from a face in the bamboo - a carved wooden mask with a mane of dried grass, worn on the back of a head.
Kurup explains, one finger up: tigers hunt by stealth from behind, and will not attack if they think you are watching. Dvij and Bhavi listen.
Bhavi, finger raised, says they should all wear masks like it.
Kurup, teeth bared, says there is no time to make so many.
Dvij, holding up two fingers, suggests strapping their backs together.
Bhavi, furious, imagines running like that with a tiger behind them.
Kurup pushes through the undergrowth, saying they must decide quickly.

A run of tall panels: the three of them hurrying down the bamboo trail, then breaking into a sprint, then Kurup falling through open sky into a deep cut in the ground - and at the bottom, Ponga and the yogini sitting unhurt among the dead leaves.
Bhavi, hands out, asking where they have gone; then Dvij looking round, saying they have vanished.
Down in the ravine: steep earth walls, a floor of dry leaves. Bhavi steadies herself against the bank while Dvij hauls Kurup up; the yogini and Ponga sit further along.
Dvij tells Bhavi she should thank the yogini; Bhavi asks - for leading them into a ditch?
Kurup crawls along the ravine floor, looks up, and announces with a raised finger that it is not a ditch but a ravine.
Dvij, looking up the cut: if a stream made this, it came from Mount Dronagiri, so the ravine must run up to the base of the mountain.
Bhavi works it out - they can travel through the forest inside the ravine and reach the mountain.
Bhavi and Kurup further along, talking about how rivers meet obstacles and change course.
Dvij, close, says he supposes he is like that himself - gone underground somewhere and turned up here.
Bhavi answers that rivers which go underground become folklore, and names stop mattering.
Kurup, delighted, calls it the perfect solution.
Three small panels: Dvij starting to say she really should; Dvij leaning to Bhavi's ear with a hand cupped, finishing - thank the yogini; and Bhavi glaring while he grins.

The party walks up the ravine between high earth walls with the light at the top: Bhavi and Dvij in front, Kurup behind, Ponga further back, the yogini striding ahead with her spear, the black dog trotting alongside.
The ravine opens out. Huge rounded boulders lie strewn where the mountain meets the plain; Dvij stands on top of one looking out, the others below with the dog.
Dvij jumps down from the boulder; Bhavi steadies herself below.
Dvij says they will take a small detour; Bhavi says they have to keep moving.
Dvij, with Kurup behind him, promises they will be back soon.
The rest of the party hurrying on among the rocks.

The Mahavidya temples: a dense cluster of carved stone spires behind a tall iron gate, orange flags on their finials, trees crowding between them. Bhavi stands with a hand on her hip asking why they are here; Dvij walks in through the gate.
Bhavi, hand out, asks why they are here; Dvij raises a finger - to meet the head pujari.
Bhavi, arms folded, says the pujari is old and reticent and meets nobody; Dvij walks on, saying he will meet them.

Inside: a hall painted from floor to ceiling with the ten Mahavidyas, each named in Devanagari - Kali dancing in flames, Tara, Bhairavi, Dhumavati, Bagalamukhi, Chhinnamasta holding her own severed head, Bhuvaneshvari - with a red Sri Yantra over the inner doorway and oil lamps burning on the floor. Dvij and Bhavi walk through it.
Bhavi turns to Dvij beneath the painted Kali, saying she has never understood the Shaktas, other than that they worship Devi.
Under the painted Kali, Dvij explains to Bhavi that for the Shaktas Devi is the ultimate Godhead.
A narrow panel of Dvij walking on past the murals.
Bhavi, close, quoting the line about Shiva unable to stir unless united with Shakti.
Outside in the sunlight, Dvij puts a hand up to a turbaned attendant who blocks the way with his palm raised.
Bhavi turns, uncertain.
At the administrator's desk: a heavy man in a dhoti with three lines of ash across his brow leans on the counter among ledgers and lamps, dismissive. Dvij and Bhavi stand before him.
Dvij and Bhavi outside; then a tall burly bearded man comes in, starts at the sight of them, and steps in on their behalf while the administrator turns away.

The inner chamber: the head pujari, very old and thin, reclines on a low couch with a rudraksha mala at his throat while an attendant fans him with a long-handled fan. Dvij and Bhavi stand barefoot before him.
Dvij, close, asking for the pujari's presence because it is true knowledge they seek; and the pujari's face in close-up, ash stripes on his brow, answering.
Dvij points back at Bhavi and tells the pujari they are going up Mount Dronagiri and that she is coming with them.
A close-up of Bhavi, uneasy at being spoken for.
A close-up of the old pujari, eyes sliding sideways - I see.
Dvij and Bhavi standing together before the couch while the pujari listens, the shrine figures dim behind them.
Dvij points at Bhavi again, saying they must not let her get hurt; Bhavi looks away; the pujari watches from behind.
The pujari leans back on his bolster and nods, eyes closed, as if he had understood everything; the attendant stands over him.
The attendant stops fanning and shows Dvij and Bhavi out through the doorway.
One last look back through the closing door at the reclining pujari, a brass lion-head ring on the door.
Bhavi rounds on Dvij outside among the temple spires - don't ever do that again.
Dvij, amused, asks what - unnerved by the old pujari?
Bhavi, finger raised, says she does not like being pointed out.
Dvij promises, never again.
Bhavi, still angry, asks what that was about her getting hurt.
Dvij, close, says nobody, and that he made use of it.

The party reunited among the boulders at the mountain's foot: Kurup with his hands on his hips, exasperated; Ponga leaning on his pole; the yogini with her spear; Bhavi and Dvij arguing; the black dog on a rock; the temple spires small below.

A run of tall panels: the group climbing a stony path in single file with the dog, up through zigzag switchbacks, until the sun goes down behind the ridges and they are strung out along the slope in silhouette.
Dvij, looking up the mountain, says it is getting late and they should find a place for the night; then Kurup, in close-up, says there is a ruined temple a few hundred yards ahead.
Bhavi, eyes closed, sweat on her face, says perfect; and the party turns uphill towards the temple, Dvij gesturing, Kurup leading, the yogini and Bhavi following.

The ruined temple at sunset: tiers of carved stone galleries broken open to a burning orange sky, trees growing out of the walls, the mountain beyond. The party comes up the slope towards it - Kurup, Bhavi, Dvij, the yogini, Ponga trailing.
Three panels of arrival: Kurup feeling his way along a wall, the yogini looking up into the ruin with her spear, Ponga settling himself on a fallen block.
Making camp: sleeping bags unrolled, Dvij and the yogini building a fire, a vessel set to boil, Kurup handing round copper mugs, Ponga at the right.
The whole party sitting round the fire clinking copper mugs, the dog curled among them, the ruined arches above.

Kurup holds forth with both hands. Beside him, a painted plate of Mount Meru: a golden peak ringed by seven coloured concentric continents and oceans under a starry sky. Dvij and Bhavi sit listening with their mugs; the yogini and Ponga at the right.
A close-up of Bhavi's hair and earring.
Bhavi, half smiling, asks whether jambu means jamun; Dvij looks up, caught by the idea. Beside them, the Meru plate again with its rings of ocean spreading under the stars.
Kurup, hands wide, explains the river of jamun juice - the Jambunadi; Bhavi sits beside him at the fire.
Dvij slips away with a burning torch, then holds it up against a carved wall of gods and dancers.
Dvij, torch in hand, gestures at the ruin and asks what this temple is; Bhavi crouches at the fire, the yogini and Ponga behind.

Kurup, finger raised, says it was the temple of the priest of the Kushwaha kings, and that sage Drona is said to have meditated on this mountain. Two insets: a man at a stepped well, and a seated sage before a snow peak.
Dvij points away down the ruin and says he guesses this is where Kurup picked up the statue for the Professor; Kurup stands beside him.
Kurup, close, admits it is.
Dvij, close, asks why the other of only two such statues is missing.
Kurup holds up a broken figure of a celestial nymph, saying the locals must have damaged it.
Dvij crouches to set the damaged statue back on its pedestal.
Dvij at a doorway of the ruin, looking out at the stream below - he is going out to listen to it.
Kurup, from the ground, warns him to listen as much as he likes but not to drink: the water is like poison.
Bhavi gets up from the fire and hurries after him; the yogini stays with the dog.
A night gorge: a waterfall dropping into a rocky stream under a violet sky. Dvij and Bhavi walk down towards the water while he recites what he wants to see.
Bhavi claps a hand over his mouth, laughing; Dvij's eyes go wide.
Her hand still over his mouth, Dvij looking sideways at her.
Dvij's face as she takes her hand away; beside him in italic script, the thought that it should have been a kiss that stopped the kitsch.
Bhavi walks out into the shallow water ahead of him, looking back; Dvij follows.
A strip of three panels of their feet in the water, stepping close, apart, and close again.
Two panels of their hands, almost touching.
Hands brushing, fingers felt; and their two faces, not speaking.
A close-up of their hands in the mist; and Dvij and Bhavi looking at each other.
A late mist has come down over everything; the two of them are only shapes in the fog above the water.
Dvij and Bhavi in the misty gorge below the waterfall. An inset at the top shows the next clue on the parchment: a coiled serpent drawn in faded ink.
Dvij close, with the serpent drawing beside him: it cannot be Sheshnag, as there is no Krishna dancing on top.
Bhavi, close, asks why he is not photographing any of it. An inset shows a dark phone screen.
A phone held in the hand, screen blank - saving battery in case he catches a signal higher up.
Dvij and Bhavi looking off into the dark together.
Bhavi points across the water and asks about a structure over there - a temple?
Dvij crosses the stream on a fallen log with Bhavi clinging to his arm behind him, white water below.
Safe on the far bank, the two of them stand looking at each other, Bhavi with a hand on her hip.
The two push through hanging vines - Bhavi holding a knife, Dvij leading - towards an old temple almost buried in creeper, its tower black against the last light.
Inside, Dvij raises his phone torch to a carved wall where a celestial figure stands in relief; Bhavi follows him in.
The torch beam travels along a long carved panel of intertwined figures, couples and attendants; Bhavi stands at the end of it looking back at him.
Dvij lights another stretch of carved wall; Bhavi crouches beside him.
The beam moves along the frieze, panel after panel of entwined figures, Bhavi small against the wall.

The inner shrine: a headless goddess seated with her knees drawn up and a lotus where her head should be, surrounded by carved elephants and attendant figures. Dvij holds up the light and names her - Lajja Gauri. Bhavi stands at the right.
The two of them in a moonlit doorway, faces almost touching, her hand at his chest.
Dvij and Bhavi close together - and behind them in the dark doorway, a figure watching.
Bhavi pulls him to her and kisses him; the figure still stands in the passage behind.
A narrow strip of the ruined corridor.
The two of them walking back through the night forest towards the campfire, not touching.
Three stacked close-ups: Bhavi saying she did that to spite that woman, Dvij saying he knows, and Bhavi telling him he is what her uncle would call a gandharva's incarnation.

Dvij asleep by the fire, and above him a vision: a figure with a column of golden light rising from the base of the spine. Beside it, the Professor in a dream-cloud surrounded by five emblems - a cup, a fish, meat, a hand gesture, a couple. And finally, a coiled golden serpent of light standing over the sleeping Dvij.

Dawn on the mountain: the party climbing a wet path through dripping forest, the sun coming up over the ridges. Dvij and Bhavi behind, Ponga and the yogini in the middle, Kurup out in front pointing the way.
Kurup points away from the water, arguing for the longer but safer route; Bhavi stands with her arms folded, Ponga leans on his pole, Dvij faces him, the yogini waits with her spear.
Dvij, seen from behind, points up the rushing stream - they need to cover ground and will follow the water.
Bhavi, half smiling; and below her, Dvij asking whether she is charmed.
Bhavi, denying it flatly; and below, Dvij grinning at her.
Dvij and Bhavi walking on beside the stream, the others ahead; he teases that he will not tell her what the coiled serpent means, and she says he knows he will.

Dvij and Bhavi crouched over his notes on a rock by the water. Between them, a chart of the kundalini: a seated figure with the seven chakras up the spine - muladhara, svadhisthana, manipura, anahata, vishuddha, ajna, crown - the sushumna channel marked, and a serpent coiled at the base.
Bhavi holds up a sheet with an elephant drawn on it and names it - Vishuddha, the throat chakra.
Dvij, delighted - bingo.

A wide mountain vista: jagged peaks, a rushing stream, and a hillside ablaze with flowering trees. Dvij and Bhavi come up the path with Ponga, the yogini and the dog; Kurup flings an arm towards the flowers and tells them the Ashtomis live up there - a race that survives by smelling flowers, and dies of any unpleasant smell. A dream-cloud above shows women with flower crowns breathing in blossom.
Bhavi stops on the path; the water below is darker at one point than elsewhere.
Dvij raises a finger to his lips - keep moving.
The two of them wading barefoot up the stream, trousers rolled, the mountain ahead.
Bhavi crouches at the bank, appalled, where a pipe emerges from the earth and spews sludge into the water.
Bhavi stands over the pipe with a hand on her hip, asking who is dumping effluent and from where.
Dvij's guess: an industrial setup on the other face of the mountain. Above them, an inset of a factory with smoking chimneys beyond the ridge.
Bhavi, arms folded, says this is why people are falling sick and they must do something; Dvij answers that they will, when the time is right - for now, pretend they know nothing about the spill.
The group moving again up the path, Dvij now walking at Kurup's side in conversation; Bhavi behind them.
A tangle of legs: Dvij's foot hooks Kurup's ankle.
Kurup pitches forward with both arms out; Dvij catches him by the arm, Bhavi watching from behind.
Dvij holds out a steel flask - here, water, filled fresh from the stream just now. Kurup, winded, takes it.
Kurup drinks deeply from the flask while Dvij watches him and Bhavi looks on from the right.

Vidgati's shrine at the end of the second day: a whole plateau carved out of the mountainside, tier on tier of pillared galleries and cave mouths cut into the rock, a flowering tree growing over a carved shrine at the centre, small houses below. The party arrives at the edge of it in the sunset, dusty and tired.
Dvij and Bhavi at the foot of a carved doorway cut into the cliff, a flowering tree overhanging it.

A carved celestial woman standing against a tree trunk with roots grown round her feet; and beside her, Dvij and Bhavi sitting on the stone floor with the parchment spread between them under the pillared gallery at dusk. Bhavi asks what the eight dancing figures are; an inset enlarges the row of eight small figures.
Dvij, close, says he thought they were wriggling tadpoles.
Dvij and Bhavi head to head over the parchment; she tells him to hush - they know the figures are eight of a kind.
The two of them crouched over the parchment in the cave hall, a hurricane lamp burning beside it and the row of figures enlarged again. Dvij asks - eight of what?
Dvij, hand open, suggests the Ashtalakshmis; beside him a plate of eight seated goddesses on lotuses.

Bhavi, finger raised, counters with the ashtamangalas - a plate of eight auspicious signs: a conch, a parasol, a lotus, a vase, two fish, the endless knot, a pot and a wheel - but says there is no connection to chakras.
Dvij looks at the next clue on the parchment: a pocket watch drawn beside a question mark.
Bhavi, chin on her fist, studying the same drawing.

A long feast in the cave hall: villagers packed round a low table heaped with dishes, lamps burning among them, jugs of wine going from hand to hand. Dvij reaches for a cup, Bhavi laughs beside him, Kurup grins across the table, Ponga eats with both hands, the yogini sits at the end. The line about living joyously while life is yours floats above the crowd.
The table itself: brass lamps among bowls of meat, rice and fruit, hands reaching in from every side.
A robed teacher sits against a carved wall and expounds Samkhya to Dvij and Bhavi. Behind him, the twenty-four principles are cut into the stone in rows, flowing from Prakriti.
Dvij jumps up pointing at the wall - that's it! - and a row of eight small figures on the carving lights up. Bhavi and the teacher look round.
Bhavi, alarmed, asks what is wrong with him; and the teacher tells them to go to the reading room in the morning.
An oil lamp burning; Dvij with a hand clapped over his own mouth, having asked out loud where he can read Charvaka's works; and Bhavi and the teacher exchanging a look.
Dvij tells Kurup, flatly, that the water he drank from his bottle was poisoned from the polluted stream. Bhavi stands between them; Kurup sits on the ground.
Kurup gets up and hurries off with a hand raised, saying something about being tired.
Kurup scrubbing at his feet in a basin; then two small frames of the party watching him go and of Dvij standing there grinning.
Bhavi slips out at night between the huts, her shawl round her.

Bhavi at Dvij's doorway, half hidden by the curtain, asking what that was with Kurup; Dvij, startled awake, says she scared him, and she tells him to say what he is hiding - he answers that someone will be missing in the morning.
A narrow panel of the dark doorway.
Dvij lying back with a hand on his full stomach, smiling. Beside him, the kundalini diagram again, lit now as far as the third chakra at the solar plexus.

Morning: Bhavi comes out of her hut to find the commotion over and Dvij leaning on a wall chewing a datoon twig. She asks who is missing; he says uh-huh; she tells him he had better explain, and fast.
Bhavi reaches for Dvij's face; he moves her hand away and walks off down the path.
Dvij, one finger raised, holding a clay cup: it's Kurup - he has absconded.
Two small frames: Dvij sluicing water over his head from a jar, and cupping it to his face. He says he will explain.
Dvij washing his face while Bhavi stands over him with her fist ready; then Dvij laughing as he straightens up.
Bhavi, holding a cup in both hands, furious - what!

A chain of small panels with arrows: a clear mountain stream, the outfall pipe running into it, the stream widening into a lake, a sick cow, and villagers tending a man lying ill. Below, in the village eating house, Dvij explains across a table that the stream carries the toxins to the lake, poisoning the land, livestock and people, and that it has lost its healing bacteriophages to chemical contamination. Bhavi listens with a steaming cup.

Two framed panels with an arrow between them: Dvij sticking out a foot to trip Kurup at the streamside, and then offering him the flask, which Kurup drinks from. Below, Dvij at the table telling Bhavi he tripped him deliberately to preoccupy him, then offered him water he said he had filled from the stream, to see whether he would drink it.
Bhavi and Dvij close together, she holding her cup, both grim.
Dvij says Kurup drank it straight down - because he knew the water was safe at that point, since he knows the pipe is downstream.

Three framed images: a bronze dancing figure on a museum stand, a portrait and a smaller statue in an interior, and the same figure standing among ruined pillars. Below, Dvij tells Bhavi across the table that the statue Kurup showed in the temple was not the one in the Professor's study - the mudras of the hands and feet differ - and that the other sits in the Mahant's stateroom, where he saw it while waiting.
Bhavi, furious, works it out: that is why he was looking at the murtis - so Kurup is the Mahant's man.
Dvij, close, lays it out: Kurup found the pipe and told the Mahant, who had been bribed by the factory owners and buried it, and offered Kurup protection. A deal was struck.

A whole wall of linked panels behind the two of them, the Mahant enthroned at the centre: Kurup found the pipe and was brought into the fold; the factory on the far side, illegal, probably mining; the drain pipe, sludge to stream, stream to lake, valley sick; sick livestock and sick people; the national park expansion whose new boundaries threaten exposure; stolen statues flowing through Kurup to the Mahant's stateroom; and at the bottom, the Park Commissioner killed in the tunnel that led to his temple. Dvij explains across the table while Bhavi holds her cup.

Bhavi, finger raised, calls the Mahant an ugly Kabandh - knowing what is causing it and letting people die. Beside her, an inset of the Kabandh: a squat headless giant with a single eye and a mouth in its belly.
Bhavi, close, says Kurup must have told the Mahant about their expedition.
Dvij answers; above them, an inset of the night procession of lamps winding up to the temple that they saw before they set out.
Dvij, close: not only that - now Kurup will share his copy of the parchment with the Mahant.
Bhavi, close, says if only she could get her hands on him.
Bhavi, arms folded, asks whether the drain pipe could be her uncle's secret; Dvij, hand open, says no - the Professor's secret is something ancient, still hidden in the parchment.

The whole parchment held up between them, its five rows clear: the eye-in-the-tree with the crescent and three discs; Ganesha with the row of eight small figures and the scattered leaves; the coiled serpent, the pocket watch and a small sketch; and the bull standing at the foot. Bhavi says there is only one thing to do - solve the rest of the clues. Mount Dronagiri fills the window behind them.
Kurup walks back down to a camp of white tents pitched at the base of the mountain, one of them grander than the rest with orange flags flying.
He stops outside the grand tent, its gilded posts and red hangings lit by a torch, a guard standing by.
Kurup at the curtain, afraid to go in.

A torch burning at the entrance; and inside, the Mahant reclining on a low bed with a lamp and a bottle beside him, pointing at Kurup and calling him a fool, while the moustached man stands at the right with his arms folded.
A close-up of Kurup, terrified: they found out about the drain pipe.
The moustached man strikes him across the face.
Kurup goes down and the moustached man stands over him.
The liquor bottle knocked flying, its contents spilling out in the air, a hand reaching after it.
The Mahant, snarling, says he told Kurup to bring him the parchment.
The moustached man, furious - where is it?
Kurup, on the ground, says he has a copy with him.
Kurup hands the rolled copy over by lamplight, saying they have solved just the first couple of clues.
The Mahant holds the roll up and unrolls it.
Kurup says they can solve the rest before them; the Mahant, sitting on the bed with the bottle, asks whether he can solve them now.
The Mahant, close, lamp beside him: Kurup said they are looking for a leaf - what leaf?
Kurup's bare legs shaking where he stands on the carpet.
Kurup, scarred and sweating, says they have not figured that out yet.
A big close-up of the Mahant, eyes sliding sideways: for Kurup's sake, he had better not be lying.
The Mahant flicks a hand from his bed - now leave, and do not show your face again. The moustached man stands with his arms folded; Kurup backs off.
Kurup hurries out of the tent into the daylight, the mountain ahead of him.
The Mahant, seen from behind, tells the moustached man to send a party forward - a little scare, not really hurt them, just delay their progress.
The moustached man nods and steps out through the tent flap; the Mahant sits on the bed behind him.

The Mahant studies the copied parchment by lamplight, a glass in his other hand, his own face reflected in it. Down the side, his thoughts in italic: these drawings could mean anything, and yet the young ones have solved them; this Dvij - who is he; could providence have brought him here; is this an omen; I must not delve into my fears, I am Mahant and I shall defy providence if need be.

The reading room: a long T-shaped hall built entirely of bamboo, its shelves slung from the ceiling on coir ropes to defeat the termites, manuscript boards hung between them, readers cross-legged on the floor in shafts of dusty light. A man in a waistcoat shows Dvij and Bhavi in.
Dvij and Bhavi sit on the floor over an open manuscript, talking.
Bhavi, finger raised, asks what made him so desperate to see this library.
A diagram from the text: five nested rings labelled niyati, raga, vidya, kaala and kala round a core of pure consciousness, with an arrow from the kaala ring to a drawn pocket watch.

Dvij explains, cross-legged: kaala is the kanchuka of time limitation, and the stopwatch points to a kanchuka - but they need a lookup table to find which chakra. Bhavi listens with a hand at her chin.
Hours later: books strewn over the floor, a lamp burning, Dvij sitting patiently while Bhavi lies flat on her face across an open volume, yawning.
Dvij, cheerful, says they will have to if she wants to crack the code.
Bhavi with her head down on the book, eyes half shut.
Dvij explains that each chakra has a bija akshara - a letter set at the centre of its lotus.
Bhavi sits up, awake at last: in the periodic table of tattvas, kaala is mapped to the letter J.

Two open pages side by side: a grid of tattvas with letters A to Z, kaala marked against J; and a chart of the seven chakras with their bija letters, svadhishthana ringed against J. Dvij names it - J is the bija akshara of svadhishthana, the sacral chakra - and beside them a glowing orange lotus seal appears. Both of them throw their arms up: two pictures cracked, only one more to go.
Dvij and Bhavi sitting on the floor of the reading room. Bhavi asks what if the Mahant's men catch up; Dvij says they will not be able to hurt her. An inset above shows a lightning-lit mountain.
Bhavi asks how he can say that with such confidence; Dvij, looking away, says he has made provisions.

A vast view from a precipice over the whole valley: brown hills giving way to green, the blue lake at the centre, temple towers scattered across the fields, a fort on the far ridge, wheat and barley in squares below. Dvij and Bhavi stand at the edge with the round-nosed man, Dvij asking him about the significance of the number eight.

The round-nosed man counts it out with framed illustrations above him: the Trimurti of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva; the four Vedas as palm-leaf bundles; and the seven of the Rig Veda's heptads. Dvij and Bhavi listen.
Bhavi, impatient - yes, yes, but how about eight?

The round-nosed man answers: the Ashtamatrikas, the Varaha Purana counting Yogeshwari as the eighth, representing the eight immoral qualities. Above them runs a frieze of the eight mother goddesses, each on her mount.
Bhavi, eyes closed, quietly pleased.

A wheel diagram of the Saptamatrika: seven goddesses set round the rim, each with a group of consonants beside her; and a painted row of the seven with their names. Below, Dvij and the round-nosed man work through it while Bhavi watches - the consonants of the alphabet are grouped into seven vargas, each belonging to one of the Saptamatrikas.
Dvij, a finger at his chin, asks - and the eighth one?
The round-nosed man throws up his hands: why, the group of vowels, of course. Dvij shouts that that is it, and Bhavi grins behind him.
Dvij throws an arm up in triumph at the precipice; the round-nosed man and Bhavi beside him, the valley spread below.
Dvij, hand on his chest, thanks the round-nosed man - twice in two days he has shown them the right path.

Back in the reading room, Dvij reaches up to a painted chart: the blue many-petalled lotus of Vishuddha at the top, with the other six chakra lotuses ranged beneath it, each named and lettered. Bhavi sits below with a hand at her chin.
Dvij points at the Vishuddha lotus and explains that the vowels are all assigned to the petals of that one lotus; Bhavi, at the right, says that is it - they have solved all of them.
Three glowing chakra seals float between them, numbered one, two and three: Vishuddha, Svadhishthana, and Vishuddha again. Bhavi says that does not seem right; Dvij sits with a hand at his chin.
Bhavi, delighted, points at an open plate: an elephant with seven trunks over the muladhara seal, labelled the base chakra. Dvij leans in beside her.
Dvij, close, asks whether those are trunks - he thought the Professor's hands were shaking when he drew it.
Bhavi, laughing, says clearly seven trunks: a seven-trunked elephant maps to muladhara, the base chakra.
Dvij, working it through: so the three chakras are muladhara, svadhishthana and vishuddha.
The two of them bent over a sheet where the three seals are laid out in an upside-down triangle, as the Professor drew it, a lamp beside them.
Bhavi scratches her head, baffled; Dvij, close, stares at the design. Neither of them can make sense of it from any angle.
Dvij sketches something on the sheet beside the three seals while Bhavi watches by lamplight.
Dvij throws his head back laughing, a hand on his stomach - he knows he should not laugh, but that is one funny face.
Bhavi shoves him away and marches off with the sheet, apologising over her shoulder.

Out at the viewpoint, Bhavi holds up the second diagram - a square, a crescent and a circle arranged as a face - and the round-nosed man names them: three homa-kundas, the fire altars. Below, a plate of two of them, the domestic fire and the oblation fire, with the southern fire beneath.

A large plate of Sulba geometry: an altar plan with a right triangle and the theorem written beneath, three fire pits drawn in section - square, round and half-moon - and a row of ancient scholars with a globe and scrolls. The round-nosed man explains that a number of mathematical discoveries were made to create these precise altar shapes, including what is known as the Pythagoras theorem. Dvij and Bhavi listen on either side.
Bhavi, holding the drawing, asks whether there is any place with such homa-kundas.
The round-nosed man answers: the ashram of Kritya Rishi, right on the path toward the top. Dvij, finger raised, asks whether the ashram has these homa-kundas.
The round-nosed man raises a finger - no doubt about it, it is a Vedic ashram after all. Above him, a thought-cloud of the ashram: a tiled roof among trees with a stepped altar in front of it.
Bhavi, pleased with herself, asks how that is for solving a clue.
Dvij, looking away, says he never doubted her drawing.
Dvij points off along the ridge - good, now they move in that direction. Bhavi stands beside him with a hand on her hip, the valley falling away below.
The party climbing a bare stony path high on the mountain, snow ranges opening out behind them: Ponga and the dog at the back, the yogini with her spear, Dvij and Bhavi ahead.
Dvij crouches at a mountain stream to drink, a torrent of white water beside him.
The four of them strung out along the path, the yogini looking back, Ponga struggling at the rear.
Ponga hunched under his pack; Bhavi glancing back over her shoulder.
Bhavi, seen from behind, watches Dvij climbing ahead of her up the rock.
The yogini stops on the path and turns; Bhavi, behind her, looks up too.
Dvij's figure on the skyline above; then the path empty where he had been.
Bhavi and the yogini, both wide-eyed, seeing him vanish.
The yogini sprints up the slope; Bhavi runs after her; and a dark chasm opens in the rock.
The two of them reach the lip of the ravine and look over.
Far below, Dvij hangs from a cluster of aerial fig roots over the drop, the yogini looking down from the rim.
Bhavi lies flat at the edge and stretches her arm down; it falls short by inches, Dvij hanging below.
The yogini crouches at the rim, sawing at the roots with a blunt knife.
Bhavi and the yogini kneel face to face at the edge, their eyes meeting over the cut roots.
Two small frames of the two women knotting the cut roots together and lowering them.
Two frames of Dvij gripping the root rope on the rock face.
Dvij climbing, then hauling himself over the lip on his front, spent.
All three sprawled at the edge, too exhausted to move: Bhavi on her back, Dvij flat out between them, the yogini beside him.
Ponga's face appears over the edge, white-bearded and inquisitive.
Dvij, lying between the two women, thanks them - he never thought they would shed their differences.
Bhavi sits up, arms folded, and the yogini stands with her spear.
Dvij, still down, finishes it - just to save me.
The yogini smiles, the first time he has seen her do so; Bhavi turns away.
Bhavi gives him her dagger-like stare and starts walking back down the slope, Dvij calling after her.
Bhavi walking away down the ridge; she looks back, ever so slightly.
Dvij and Bhavi facing each other on the path. A small scoreboard in the corner: Bhavi 2, Yogini 1.
Dvij, close, says he should thank her for saving his life; and Bhavi, below, says he did thank - both of them.
Dvij, close, says he had to, both of them helped; Bhavi answers that this time, yes, but she has saved him once already.
A shout from behind. Three men come out of ambush with daggers in their outstretched hands; Dvij and Bhavi spin round, and the yogini has already closed with one of them.
The yogini has a man down, her knife at his throat.
Dvij whips out a handgun. The thugs stop where they stand; he tells Bhavi to get behind a boulder while he holds them.
Dvij with the gun levelled, the three men backing off among the rocks, Bhavi behind him.
Bhavi crouched behind the boulder as a thug comes round it with a dagger raised.
A tall stranger in a blue kurta and red sash appears from nowhere and knocks the thug back with a blow.
The stranger grapples the thug to the ground; Dvij fires past them.
Dvij runs up the slope with an attacker after him.
Bhavi and the yogini, both alarmed, watching them go.
The two men vanish over the rim; Bhavi and the yogini run after them.
Bhavi and the yogini reach the edge and look down.
Dvij hanging from the same cluster of aerial roots, for the second time that day.
Dvij hanging from the roots again, looking up; Bhavi and the yogini at the rim above.
Two frames of the two women hauling on the root rope at the edge.
Two frames of Dvij climbing the rope up the rock face.
Dvij pulling himself over the lip; and the three of them sitting together on the rocks afterwards.
Dvij, an inset beside him showing a figure chasing another up the slope, saying he was chasing a thug away.
Bhavi, with a matching inset, says she saw someone chasing him - it looked as if both fell in.
Bhavi, chin on her hand, wonders aloud who the tall stranger was who fought on their side.
A stony gully seen from above.
Ponga lying on his back on the path where the thugs attacked him.

The party resting in the shade of the fig tree whose aerial roots have now saved Dvij twice: Dvij sitting against the rock, Ponga propped beside him, the dog at their feet, the yogini and Bhavi across from them, snow peaks framed in the gorge beyond.
Dvij trickling water from a cup into Ponga's mouth to bring him round.
Bhavi, hand at her chin, says she gets that he lured the thug to the ravine - but why did he jump in?
Dvij says he forgot about the ravine; Bhavi tells him he forgot about the ravine where he had almost died a few moments ago, and that that is stupid.
Dvij, sitting back against the rock, says not for someone who has forgotten his whole past.

The quiet evening walk: the party crossing a high open field at nightfall towards a dolmen - three upright stones under a great capstone - its shadow thrown long by the last light, snow peaks all round.

Camped under the dolmen by a small lamp, Bhavi lying propped on her elbows and Dvij sitting against the stone. He says the Mahant needs them to get him close enough to the secret of the leaf, and will keep following until then. Beside them, an inset of a line of torches winding up the mountain.
Dvij, close, says who knows what he might do after that.
Bhavi, close, says he is scaring her.
An inset of Dvij taking a pistol from a firearm display case in the Park Commissioner's bungalow; below, Dvij sits turning the gun over by lamplight while Bhavi watches.
Dvij, close, says he thought it would come in useful on a day like this.
Bhavi, close, asks how he knows so much about guns.

The dolmen at night under a field of stars, the lamp burning between them, Ponga asleep at the left and the dog curled up beside him. Bhavi's thought floats above her: there is a fifty percent chance that he is a good guy.

A flashback in Bhavi's memory: the Park Commissioner's gun room, a rack of muskets, flintlocks, a derringer, a howdah pistol and a Colt revolver in a glass case. Dvij polishes the glass with a cloth while Bhavi stands behind him.
Dvij lifts a revolver out of the case, checking its action with a fluency he cannot account for; Bhavi holds up a phone light behind him.
Dvij shoulders a rifle and explains the grooves that spin the bullet for accuracy at longer range; Bhavi stands with her arms folded.
Dvij swings the barrel round towards her; Bhavi, unimpressed, says she would care more for that if the gun were not pointed at her face.

A second flashback, in the Professor's study: charts of the brain and a board comparing semantic memory - knowing how to drive a car, how to use a gun - with episodic memory, where and when you learned. The Professor lectures with books piled round him while Dvij listens.

A strip of small frames: a car, a drink, a coil of rope, a figure in the forest, a rope bridge, an old book, a jigsaw with a piece missing. The Professor, finger raised, tells Dvij he has clearly retained his semantic memory - he knows about computers, mobiles, the internet, things that do not exist in this valley.

The Professor, finger up, tells him to go out and listen to the forest and the rumbling hills, and that his body will tell him what he knows until he has the complete picture of himself. Two insets below: Bhavi frowning, and Dvij half smiling.
Back under the dolmen at night: Bhavi lies awake beside the lamp, Dvij sitting against the stone looking out at the stars. Her thought: what picture do I have of him?
Dvij, close, half smiling: don't worry about the gun, there are no bullets.
Bhavi sits up, shocked - that was weighing on her mind, and good he took them out.
Dvij, smiling to himself, says he did not take them out; there never were any.
Bhavi rounds on him where they sit by the lamp - he was bluffing with their lives at stake?
Under the dolmen at night: Ponga asleep at the left, Bhavi and Dvij sitting up talking, the yogini keeping watch at the right with her spear. Dvij says it is a good thing she is with them.
Bhavi, close, looking away, saying that when he was brought to the lodge he was still conscious despite all the blood he had lost.
Bhavi and Dvij lying face to face under the stone, close together; she says that like the tantric baba said, the yogini must have done something that kept him alive - and that both of them helped.
Dvij, close, looking up.
The two of them lying side by side looking up at the Milky Way - shooting stars, but so many?
The dolmen from a distance under a vast starry sky, standing in a field thick with fireflies, its fire a small glow beneath the stone.

A run of narrow panels as everything goes quiet: the dolmen under the stars, the stream, the tall grass, the yogini sitting up with her spear, a bare tree, and Dvij and Bhavi awake in the dark. He asks whether she hears that.
Dvij looking up, a column of golden light and a bright seal at the heart glowing beside him; Bhavi asleep at his shoulder. He names it - Anahata, the sound of the unstruck.
Dvij walks out from the dolmen into the field of fireflies under the Milky Way, leaving Bhavi asleep under the stone and heading towards where the yogini lies.

Dawn under the dolmen: Dvij wrapped in a blue blanket, Bhavi crouched over a small fire with a pot on it, Ponga sitting with the dog at the right, the mountains pale behind them. Dvij says the smell of morning coffee is good enough to wake any sleeping soul.
Dvij, close, wrapped in the blanket, asking where she got the milk.
Bhavi, stirring the pot, says no milk, no sugar - dark as the devil.
Bhavi, close, says she does not see the yogini around; Dvij, wrapped in the blanket, says maybe she went back.
The two of them sitting with their coffee mugs under the dolmen at sunrise, the dog asleep between them; Bhavi asks whether she left him the mutt.

Three frames on the trail: Ponga scrambling ahead with his staff, then walking between Dvij and Bhavi, then crouching to pick at a plant while the dog watches. Bhavi asks why her uncle wanted Ponga along; Dvij says he will help them when the time comes.
Dvij holds up a drawing of a single leaf to Ponga; Bhavi watches.
Ponga's face lights up, and the leaf drawing glows in his hands.
Bhavi, worried, asks whether the thugs will attack them again.

A strip of four numbered frames of Bhavi thinking, and below, Dvij telling her that in all these years she has feared for the Professor but never for herself - and asking whether she ever wondered why.
The Vedic ashram of Kritya Rishi: bamboo-and-thatch huts round a swept clearing, swastikas over every entrance, forest and mountains behind. The party walks in.

Inside the altar hall: a square fire altar at the centre surrounded by three homa-kundas - square, circular and crescent - exactly as Bhavi had drawn them. An inset shows her sketch of the same three shapes beside two chakra seals.
The ceremony beginning: priests seated round the altars, offerings laid out, the fire lit; the udgatrus start their Samaveda chants and the sound is drawn as golden ribbons curling through the air.
More of the ceremony in small frames: singers breaking into dance, others taking up the naali and dundhubi drums, the fire building.
Outside the ashram, Bhavi moves through a garden in flower, going from tree to tree, a white blossom held to her face.

Dvij sits cross-legged before the fire opposite the Vedic sage - white-bearded, in white cloth, rudraksha at his throat - who tells him the Vedas are apaurusheya, ever-present and received by the ancient rishis. Other listeners sit behind.

A vision above them of rishis seated in golden light, with panels labelled shruti and smriti - the heard and the remembered. The sage explains that they are shrauta texts preserved by oral recitation, and that the Upanishads interpret them.
A vision of Yama enthroned, and of a river running down to the sea. The sage explains punarmrityu, re-death, and the endless cycle of samsara.

More visions: a boy before a fire, a dark doorway, a figure meditating, Yama again. The sage tells how Nachiketas learned to conquer the cycle from Lord Yama, and that as the river disappears into the sea, we become one with the divine.

A vision of a horse beside a fire, and of a horse drawn in stars with the sun for its eye. The sage explains the ashwamedha - the horse is the sun, its body is time, the sacrifice is of worldly comforts.
A split fruit, its seeds, and a hand holding nothing. The sage gives Svetaketu's lesson: split the fruit, split its seed, keep splitting - the invisible essence left at the end is Brahman.
A hand dropping salt into a bowl of water, Dvij tasting it, and a glowing figure seated in a starlit sea. The sage says Brahman can be experienced but not observed - tat tvam asi.

A chart on the wall of the four kalas of the day - morning practice, midday service and study, evening worship, night rest. Dvij thanks the sage, saying he now sees the world in a way he never had, but his mind remains restless and he will come and seek more.

Dvij and Bhavi in the flowering garden, she holding a lily to her face. She asks whether meeting the maharishi is that important; he says yes, else his mind will remain restless, and that she has heard him tell many that he seeks the truth but never thought he meant it.
Bhavi, hand at her chin, considering him.
Dvij, close among the flowers, says he did not - but now he thinks he does.
Bhavi smiling at him; Dvij smiling back, the two of them in the garden.
Dvij, hand open, gives her two things to do: first, work on the next clue.
Bhavi listening among the lilies as he adds the second - find a safe spot away from the ashram.
Dvij walking away down the path; Bhavi tells him to be careful.
Bhavi stands with the dog watching his figure recede up the path between the flowering trees; at the right, Ponga comes shuffling out of the undergrowth with his staff.
Bhavi, hand at her chin, asks herself whether she is in love.

Bhavi, eyes closed, answering herself - how can I know? And beside her, a whole column of thought bubbles crowding up the mountainside: Kurup the two-faced coward; uncle's condition; the yogini's disappearance; Dvij's strange smile; the Mahant's rage; what if his cell catches a network at the top, will he leave me for good? And at the bottom: focus, Bhavi, focus.

A path circling high above the ashram, the temple and huts small in the valley below. Bhavi points out three large boulders leaning together - they will rest under them tonight. Ponga sits on a rock behind her with the dog.
Bhavi, close, telling herself to focus.
Bhavi crouches with the parchment open beside Ponga in the shelter of the boulders, asking about the next clue - nine green eyes, and why are they splotchy?
Ponga, close, mumbling incoherently.
Bhavi, half smiling - she will take that as a yes.
Bhavi holds the parchment up: she says those stems in her uncle's room, the green is from pressed stem ends.
Bhavi, holding the parchment, with Ponga behind her: these cannot be eyes - maybe something they eat, small, round, bean-shaped.
Two framed images in her thought: a bundle of green stems, and one of the splotchy shapes enlarged on the parchment.
Bhavi, delighted, holds the parchment up with the row of green beans clear on it - beans, green beans, moong. Even the maharaj could tell that. Ponga grins beside her.
Bhavi holds the parchment up, triumphant, beside Ponga among the boulders - I got it, Ponga.
A large close-up of Ponga, white-bearded and wild-haired, gazing up at the sky.
Bhavi, hand open, asks him to please stop staring at the heavens and help her with why nine; the parchment lies across her knees.
Nine glowing spheres hang in the sky above the gorge. Bhavi, delighted, names them - the navgrahas, the nine planets - Ponga still gazing up beside her.

Two remembered scenes: the nine grahas each on their mount in a ring, and a pujari laying out grains and offerings at a navgraha puja while a woman watches. Bhavi explains that she saw one once, that the pujari asked for green beans because it was a Wednesday, and that each navgraha has its own grain - so the clue points to Wednesday.
Bhavi, hand at her chin, worried: but which Wednesday - what day is it today, and how long has it been since they started?
A run of panels of Bhavi walking back down the mountain path towards the ashram at sunset, past Ponga sitting among the rocks - she cannot wait to see the look on Dvij's face.
Bhavi walking in the flowering garden at dusk, then stopping, then standing still - a circle, like the Laxman rekha.
Three frames of Bhavi hurrying, then running, as dark clouds gather and the birds stop.
Bhavi running full tilt through the black garden.
She runs straight into Dvij and they both go down in a scatter of fruit from his bag.
Dvij on his back with his mouth open, stars round his head; Bhavi sitting up beside him.
Bhavi laughing with a hand at her face; Dvij rubbing his head - and he thought he was scared.
Four frames of the two of them walking back together through the dark garden, musical notes drifting through the air, as Dvij names it - aranya gaana, someone singing sacred mantras in contemplation.
A large close-up of Bhavi, finger raised, announcing that she has solved the next clue - and mind you, without any of his cheat sheets.
Bhavi and Dvij walking on among the flowers with the fruit bag.
By firelight among the boulders, Bhavi points along the parchment while she explains, the bag of fruit beside her.
Dvij crouched at the fire, listening, genuinely appreciative.

The two of them working by firelight over the parchment and Dvij's charts: a plate of leaves, a casket of emeralds and a compass rose, with notes that green is too broad, an emerald is not the only gem, and that direction is what they are really being told. Dvij works it through - moong maps to Budha, but also to earth, brass and emerald.
Bhavi, close: it's a leaf, and green is bound to be everywhere.
Dvij, close, catching it - each graha presides over a direction, and Budha has north.
Bhavi says they need to move northwards, and suggests asking the ashram people for directions.
Dvij says that is too risky, since the Mahant's men will force the information out of them - they need to find north themselves.
A diagram of a gnomon on the rock beside them: the shadow's arc through the day, the noon shortest shadow pointing true north. Dvij says they will build one.
Three frames of them cutting a stake, uncoiling rope and marking out the ground.
Dvij driving the stake in and swinging the rope to scribe a circle.
The stake standing in its scribed circle at sunset; Dvij crouched over it, Bhavi watching with a hand at her chin.
The finished circle with the line drawn through it, marked north; the two of them crouched beside it.
A blazing sunset over the whole valley, Dvij marking the ground at the foot of the gnomon, Bhavi standing over him.
A strip of frames: a figure approaching in the dusk, Ponga arriving, Ponga holding out a great lump of cow dung, and Bhavi asking what he is up to.
Ponga crouched at the fire lighting the dung, Dvij laughing beside him, Bhavi at the right - it makes a good mosquito repellent, and no smell.
Dvij, close, smiling: for all his supposed insanity, the man sometimes seems saner than the rest of them.
Three narrow frames of the night sky over the boulders, clouds building.
Bhavi, close, says she is tired - good night.

The shelter under the boulders at night: Ponga tending the small fire, Bhavi asleep, Dvij lying awake. Above him on the rock, drawn in firelight: an om, a flame, a seated rishi, and a figure with the seven chakras up the spine. Dvij thinks of the power of chanting, the cleansing by Agni, the doctrine of the twice-dead, and wonders whether his kundalini has risen to vishuddha.
Dvij asleep with a hand over his mouth, yawning.
Bhavi, alarmed, looking out at the ground: the gnomon - it's gone.
The two of them out on the churned mud in the rain, the stake and rope washed away.
Dvij yawns; Bhavi glares at him.
Dvij points out over the valley at people in the fields - think of the happiness of the people in the valley; Bhavi stands with her arms folded. Beside them, the flooded ground and the ruined circle.
Dvij says it was too cloudy and would not have worked anyway; Bhavi curses the rains.
Dvij, hand open, says he thought they were desperate for rain; Bhavi puts a hand to her head - a day, couldn't the rains have waited just one more day?
Dvij, hand on his chest, tells her to chill, they'll work something out - be like Ponga, still.
Ponga sitting cross-legged in the mouth of the shelter, telling his beads by the fire.

Dvij and Bhavi sitting with Ponga at the fire. Above them, a diagram of the four states - waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and turiya at the centre - and a glowing rudraksha mala. Dvij asks where Ponga got the mala; then Ponga, Bhavi and Dvij in three close frames, and Dvij raises a finger: wait, I have an idea.
Ponga, eyes closed; and Dvij gesturing at him with both hands.
Dvij gesticulating at Ponga with a raised finger while Ponga gestures back; Bhavi watching them, astonished.
Dvij eases the rudraksha mala out of Ponga's tightly clasped hand, the old man's fingers still closed round it.
Four small frames: Dvij separating the beads, cutting a length of stalk, threading the beads along it, and binding the ends.
Dvij holds the strung bead-rod up; then it hangs from a cord; then Dvij watches it turn.
Dvij holding the rod in the cave mouth, Ponga sitting behind him.
Bhavi and Dvij watching it, Bhavi wide-eyed.

The rod hanging on its cord in the cave mouth, one rudraksha swinging beneath it with magnetic field lines drawn round it, the valley beyond. Dvij explains that rudraksha has magnetic properties and a stalk full of them will align along the earth's magnetic field.

A wide view down into the valley: a straight path running between two lines of pale flowering trees, deep forest either side, a temple spire in the distance. Bhavi points along it - so the path they must take is that one, the one flanked by bakul trees.
Dvij and Bhavi lie on the ridge above the ashram with Ponga behind them, looking down into the compound as sharp cries rise from below.
Armed men with sticks charge in and haul the bamboo huts down, the swastika over a doorway splintering.
Frightened faces at a window; the ashram dwellers wrestled down and herded together in the open.
The compound from above, the huts collapsed and the people penned in groups. The Mahant walks in flanked by the moustached man.
The Mahant strides through the seated captives towards the great banyan while a sadhu falls at his feet beseeching him; the moustached man follows at his heel.
From the ridge, the banyan and the wrecked ashram below. Dvij says it is good they did not tell the ashram people where they were going.
The Mahant kneels over the copied parchment spread on the ground, tracing its rows with both hands, three lines of ash on his brow.
Bhavi, close, watching from the rocks: he is working out the direction from the clues himself.
The Mahant's party filing out of the ashram gates in a column, heading away south. Bhavi says it looks as though he has worked it out - but why are they headed south?
Dvij, close: green maps to north, he is sure of it.
Dvij looks again at his own parchment, where the row of beans is drawn in black rather than green - that's odd, his parchment has black beans, not green.

Dvij and Bhavi crouched over the parchment among the rocks, the green beans clear on it. He asks why she is smiling; she says the original parchment has green beans. Below, a three-part diagram: Bhavi inking the copies at a table; a chart comparing the original, Dvij's copy and Kurup's copy with their bean colours and the directions north, west and south; and the Mahant's men marching off under a red arrow.
Bhavi, close, explaining that she changed the colour on each copy to sniff out their treachery.
Dvij, close, working it through: so his is black, and Kurup's must be red - which maps to south.
The two of them looking down from the rocks at the column leaving the ashram. That is why they are heading south.
A long line of men winding away down the valley path.
Dvij, delighted, snaps his fingers at her - this is brilliant, now they can never catch us.
A large close-up of Bhavi, pleased with herself: we have the Mahant out of our way.
Dvij, close: then what are they waiting for - let's go.
Bhavi smiling to herself; and below, three frames of Ponga being roused from his meditation and the two of them shouldering their packs.

The party sets off up the path that runs north from the ashram, bakul trees in white flower on either side, a temple spire below and the mountain waiting above: Dvij leading, Bhavi behind, Ponga with his bundle and staff, the dog at the rear.

Five tall frames of the climb: the path rising steeply beside a waterfall, the vegetation thinning, the air getting rarer, Dvij and Bhavi ahead and Ponga labouring behind with the dog. Dvij says the climb is like trying to find the end of Shiva's column of fire - unending; Bhavi's worry is that they are looking for a plant and have left most of them behind.
Ponga struggling under his bundle; Bhavi looking back at him - how does the old man keep going?
Dvij, half turning: his sense of purpose, he supposes. Bhavi, exhausted, says she needs a rest stop.
Dvij points up the slope. Far above, on a rocky spur, stands a small white shrine with a red base. Bhavi looks up; Ponga and the dog come up behind.

The shrine close to: white with a vermillion base, a brass Hanuman face set in its niche, a trident with a damroo at its nape planted beside it, and a great spreading tree over it. Beneath the tree an orange-robed monk sits in meditative stillness, a langur on the rock above. Dvij, Bhavi, Ponga and the dog come up the last steps.
The monk opens his eyes and raises a hand - come forth. Dvij is already climbing towards him; Bhavi and Ponga behind.
A close-up of the monk's face, shaven-headed and calm.
The monk again, faintly smiling - do not hide from yourself. Below, Dvij and Bhavi exchange a startled look.
Dvij stands before the seated monk under the tree, Bhavi coming up the steps behind him, the shrine and the langur at the right.

An inset of Dvij reaching towards a blazing light with a small glowing figure at his own chest. Below, the monk tells him he seeks the Absolute Truth and does not know that he already possesses it; Dvij and Bhavi sit listening.
An inset of Dvij, bandaged, surrounded by cloudy faces he cannot place. The monk says he has forgotten - just as an accident makes a man forget his own past.
An inset of Dvij with his palms joined before a glowing four-armed deity. The monk says it is like a devotee who seeks God and does not know God is already within him.

Two insets: a luminous figure floating in a starfield beside a drawn brain; and monks walking towards a great light while Dvij and Bhavi watch. Below, the monk explains that he is a reflection of a soul wandering in vacuum, having lost its association with the mind that makes it realise its purpose.
Dvij asks how one can renounce the world - what else is there but feelings? The monk answers: the Truth.
Dvij asks whether the monk can teach him the Truth; the monk says he can show him the way.
Dvij asks how he can reach it; the monk says he has to look within.
Later under the tree: Bhavi asleep on the rock, Dvij sitting with his phone out, the shrine beyond. The climb had drained her and she slept through most of the discourse.
Bhavi, waking, asks where the monk is; Dvij, phone in hand, says he left - and no signal either.
Dvij, close: he asked me to look within.
Bhavi, close: not before you look at the next clue. And the two of them bend over the parchment together, Bhavi pointing at the bull with two legs - oh, she knows this one, that is Dwaparayuga.
Dvij and Bhavi crouched over the parchment under the tree, her finger on the bull.
A plate of the four yuga bulls - Satyuga with four legs, Treta with three, Dwapara with two, Kali with one - as Bhavi explains that Satyuga is the complete bull.
Dvij, close, asks how she knows this; Bhavi answers that he is not the only one who reads her uncle's books.
A diagram of the Vastu Purusha: the sprawled cosmic man laid over a square, the directions round the edge and his organs labelled.
Bhavi and Dvij over the parchment - this man forms a perfect square, head at north-east, feet at south-west - and Dvij, fingers at his brow, names it: vaastu purusha, the cosmic man.
Bhavi asks what about the fish - Mina, Pisces?
Dvij leans over the parchment while Bhavi watches: the rashis preside over specific organs, Mesha the head.

A table of the zodiac against the body - Mesha head, Vrishabha neck, Mithuna arms, Karka chest, Simha heart, Kanya stomach, Tula navel, Vrischika genitals, Dhanu thighs, Makara knees, Kumbha ankles, Mina feet - and Dvij, finger raised, carrying it through to Mina the feet.
Bhavi, eyes wide: the feet of the vaastu purusha.

The two of them with the charts spread out: a Vaastu Purusha Mandala with the south-west zone marked armoury or library, and a disc of the Vedic day divided into four prahars. Bhavi holds up the mandala - vaastu places a library where the feet are, and says to be there from three to six in the pursuit of knowledge.
The same charts with the four yuga bulls and the zodiac table. Dvij adds that the Dwaparyuga bull also maps to the afternoon kala at the Vedic ashram - the third prahara, three to six.
Bhavi, chin on her hand: but what?
Dvij, hand at his chin, asks what could happen under the shade of this tree.

A chain of linked cards running down the page: two-legged bull, Dwaparyuga, third kala, 3 pm to 6 pm; fish, Mina, feet, feet of vaastu purusha, south-west zone, library - resolving at the bottom to Library, 3 pm to 6 pm. Dvij says that is double confirmation: something will happen here between three and six.
Dvij, struck by it - shadows, they will elongate and point the way. Four small frames show the sun lowering and a shadow stretching across the ground.
Dvij and Bhavi crouched on the rock, looking out at the ground.
The two of them looking across at the white shrine on its spur, then back at each other.
The shrine with the trident planted beside it, the sun high, its shadow lying across the bare ground. Bhavi, seeing it: why, it's the shadow of the trishul.
Sunset behind the shrine. Bhavi flings out an arm along the shadow - it's Lord Shiva, he will show them the way. Dvij crouches beside her.
Five tall frames as the light goes: Dvij spreading a bedspread, Bhavi laying out food, Ponga arriving, the two of them sitting to eat, and the trident's shadow lengthening across the ground in each.
Ponga sits on the spread eating wild berries by the handful and spitting the kernels out in a practised arc; Bhavi and Dvij watch him without trying to understand.
Bhavi, annoyed; Dvij, amused, at the edge of the frame.
Bhavi, hand at her chin, asks why he is punching holes in that bottle; Ponga sits working at a plastic bottle with the dog beside him.
Bhavi turns, delighted - look at the beautiful butterflies. Moths crowd the flowers in the foreground while Dvij and Ponga look on.
Three close frames: Dvij saying they're moths, Bhavi saying and beautiful, Dvij smiling at her.
Three more: Dvij, a hand to his mouth, saying he knows what the secret is; Bhavi asking how he can know that; Dvij answering - whose temple are they sitting next to?
Dvij flings out an arm, pointing, and Bhavi turns to look. The trident's shadow is stretched right across the stony ground, its tip resting in the mouth of a narrow path.
Three frames of Ponga's hands punching more holes in the plastic bottle with a spike.
Bhavi and Dvij down on their knees among the rocks searching the scrub, the dog between them, the path winding away behind.
Bhavi holds up a frond of leaves, frowning; Dvij crouches with his phone beside another plant, the Professor's leaf drawing on the screen. None of them match.

Dvij gestures at a three-step diagram - a healthy plant, the weed beside it, the weed choking it out - saying the plant must have been here earlier and this invasive species wiped it out. Bhavi sits on the ground beside him.
A close view of the weed growing thick among the stones; Bhavi with a hand to her head, dismayed; and Dvij standing with his phone, thinking.
Bhavi, close: it's not here. Dvij, close, looking down: we're doomed.
Bhavi sits slumped among the rocks with her head on her hand; Dvij stands looking out over the mountains, wishing they could take the whole mountain, like Lord Hanuman.
The dog barks up at something. Dvij turns, and high in the tree above, Ponga is sitting on a branch with a plastic bottle dangling on a string beneath him.
Ponga knots the string to the branch; below, Dvij and Bhavi stand looking up at the bottle, where a large moth is caught inside.
Dvij, close, looking up: he's got a moth in a bottle?
Bhavi, close: looks like - she wonders why.
A big close-up of Bhavi, finger raised, mouth open: pheromone trap.
Dvij, close, asks how she knew this.

Three illustrated panels - ants trailing a scent from a plant, a moth against a moonlit sky with ribbons of scent curling from it, and the bottle with moths gathering round it - while Bhavi explains that the trapped male will release chemicals like a brassy perfume and the females will come to the bottle. Dvij stands beside her with the bottle hanging in the foreground.
Bhavi, close: because she has studied biology.
Dvij, wide-eyed: oh, right - so the Professor knew they would need Ponga for this.
Five frames in a row: the bottle hanging with its moth, and moths arriving in ones and twos, then in dozens, then in a dark cloud, while Dvij and Bhavi watch from below.
A dark swarm of moths streaming over the rocks, Dvij and Bhavi small beneath the tree.
Bhavi and Dvij running uphill through the stones with the dog, the bottle still hanging behind them and the swarm pouring overhead.
Bhavi hauls Dvij up a boulder by the hand as the swarm streams past.
Bhavi climbing, Ponga struggling up behind her.
Dvij reaching back down to pull her up the last of the rocks.
The four of them and the dog reach the top of the ridge and stop: below them the swarm pours away down the chasm, and around them a whole field of white lilies is swaying in the wind.
Bhavi runs out into the field of white flowers with her arms flung wide - we did it, we did it - Dvij and the dog behind her, snow ranges beyond.
Dvij and Bhavi standing together among the lilies at sunset, she with her hands at her chest.
An inset of Hanuman flying through the clouds carrying a whole mountain. Dvij asks what herb Lord Hanuman was looking for when he carried the mountain away.
Bhavi, eyes huge, shouts the name - sanjeevani; and Dvij, smiling: exactly, the miracle plant.
Bhavi, close, asks who the tall stranger was who fought the thugs; Dvij, close, half smiling.

Two insets: the old pujari of the Mahavidya temples seated in his shrine, and the tall stranger knocking a thug down. Below, Dvij tells her he was sent by the pujari to protect her, that he is the doyen of the shakta tradition - she embodies the Goddess, and he would not let her be harmed.
Bhavi, close, asks who he really is.
Dvij, close, before he can reply - his phone is ringing, the sound carrying out into the vastness.
Five tall frames: Dvij takes the phone out at the cliff edge, looks at it, turns away, stands with it in his hand, and lets it slip from his palm. Bhavi watches him from below in each one.
The phone falling away down the sheer walls of the chasm, Dvij standing tiny on the lip above: there goes my past.
Bhavi runs to him through the flowers, then stops; she reaches out a hand and asks why; and then she has hold of his arm at the edge.
Dvij and Bhavi holding each other among the white flowers on the cliff top, rain clouds moving in over range after range of mountains. The phone is gone. The past is gone. What remains is this.
A wide cliff-top view at dusk: Bhavi stands alone under the overhanging tree among the white flowers while Dvij stands apart at the edge, looking out at range after range of snow peaks.
Three close frames: Dvij turning to her, Bhavi looking up at him, Dvij looking back.
Bhavi, both hands open, asks whether he is going to leave her alone; Dvij, seen from behind, faces her.

Dvij talks with an open hand among the flowers, Bhavi beside him. At the right, a diagram of the five sheaths: a serene face at the centre labelled atman, ringed by the annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya and anandamaya koshas.

A thought-cloud of the yogini with her spear and of the old Mahavidya pujari among his people. Dvij tells her that in the yogini she will find a true friend, and in the Mahavidya priest the strongest of allies.
A thought-cloud of the Professor addressing a gathering of tribespeople and villagers. Dvij tells her she is the only one who can stop the Mahant.

A thought-cloud of the drainpipe, of Bhavi gathering the herb, of villagers being treated, of green fields restored, and of the Mahant. Dvij lists it: close the drainpipe, rally the peasants, heal them with this herb.
A thought-cloud of villagers, of the yogini, and of Bhavi among them. Bhavi stands with her hands pressed together, listening.

Two insets: Bhavi holding a sprig of the herb over the sleeping Professor, and Dvij walking away towards the mountain. Below, Dvij tells her he is a seeker, and seekers do not become good healers - she, on the other hand, is selfless.

Dvij sits among the flowers with his eyes closed, Bhavi holding his arm. Above him rises a figure of light with the seven chakras up the spine and a column of glowing points going up into the clouds. He says his kundalini has risen to ajna, the brow chakra - but there are seven extra-sensory chakras, and he has to keep moving towards the Truth.
Three frames: Bhavi watching Dvij walk away down the path, the path itself running on through the flowers into the light, and Bhavi's face with tears in her eyes.
Dvij walking up the valley path through the white flowers, the dog following, the last of the sun ahead of him.
Rain sweeping across the flowers and the dark ranges beyond.
The village in the rain: people walking out into the flooded lanes; and then a woman and a man with their arms flung up, children and villagers laughing with their faces turned to the sky.
The valley under gathering storm clouds, a last band of gold along the horizon; and a slim black-and-white chatak bird flying up into the darkness, calling.
